question.text: Will the winner of Alaska's 2026 gubernatorial election receive fewer votes in the first round than another candidate?
question.resolution_criteria: This question resolves as **Yes** if the winner of the [2026 Alaska gubernatorial election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_Alaska_gubernatorial_election) receives fewer initial first-choice vote counts than another candidate, according to official results.

research:
## 1. Resolution source
- 2026-10-25: The resolution page is the Wikipedia article for the [2026 Alaska gubernatorial election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_Alaska_gubernatorial_election). It has no general-election results yet because the vote is on 2026-11-03. Official numbers will come from the Alaska Division of Elections' RCV round-by-round tables.
- 2026-10-25: Four candidates are on the general ballot: Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins (D), Bernadette Wilson (R), Dave Bronson (R) and Treg Taylor (R). [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_Alaska_gubernatorial_election)

## 2. Current status
- Nothing has settled the question yet.
- Kreiss-Tomkins is far ahead in first-choice polling. That means "Yes" in practice requires a Republican, most likely Wilson, to trail in round 1 but win after Bronson's and Taylor's votes transfer. So "Yes" is roughly the same event as "a Republican wins."
- A Kreiss-Tomkins win would almost certainly come with him leading round 1, which resolves "No."

## 3. Recent news (newest first)
- 2026-10-24: Former Lt. Gov. Loren Leman wrote an op-ed backing Ballot Measure 2, which would repeal RCV. Any repeal would not apply to this election. [ADN](https://www.adn.com/opinions/2026/10/24/opinion-why-ranked-choice-is-bad-for-alaska/)
- 2026-10-23: Kreiss-Tomkins, Bronson and Taylor appeared together on an AFN convention panel. [KPVI](https://www.kpvi.com/news/regional_news/gubernatorial-candidates-make-their-pitch-at-the-alaska-federation-of-natives-convention/article_b88b79fd-b1f6-5541-94fc-f0562ea1461b.html)
- 2026-10-22/23: The DOJ sued to block certification of the US Senate result over a second "Dan Sullivan" on the ballot. That suit concerns the Senate race, not the governor's race. [Fairfield Sun Times](https://www.fairfieldsuntimes.com/news/national/trump-administration-sues-to-block-alaska-election-results/article_80189f13-8d45-55f2-af66-d830223eca3e.html)
- Oct 15-18 poll, Alaska Survey Research (1,568 likely voters): round 1 was Kreiss-Tomkins 50, Wilson 30, Bronson 12, Taylor 8. Final round: Kreiss-Tomkins 55, Wilson 45. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_Alaska_gubernatorial_election)
- Oct 8-16 poll, Data for Progress (D): round 1 was Kreiss-Tomkins 49, Wilson 29, Bronson 12, Taylor 9. Final round: 53-47 for Kreiss-Tomkins, with a hypothetical scenario showing 50-50. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_Alaska_gubernatorial_election)
- 2026-10-06: Kreiss-Tomkins had raised more than his three Republican opponents combined: $2.1M versus $852K since early August. [ADN](https://www.adn.com/politics/2026/10/06/alaskas-democratic-candidate-for-governor-has-raised-more-than-his-3-republican-opponents-combined/)
- Oct 1-3 poll, ASR: round 1 was 48/27/15/10. Final round: 54-46 for Kreiss-Tomkins. Sep 24-Oct 1 poll, NYT/Siena: round 1 was 46/24/17/13. Final round: 52-48. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_Alaska_gubernatorial_election)
- Late September: Bronson and Taylor released a joint video asking Republicans to rank all three GOP candidates. [FairVote](https://fairvote.org/what-to-expect-in-alaskas-2026-ranked-choice-voting-elections/)
- 2026-09-18 and 2026-09-22: Wilson asked Bronson and Taylor to drop out. They have not. [ADN](https://www.adn.com/politics/2026/09/18/wilson-again-calls-on-her-republican-opponents-to-drop-out-of-alaska-governors-race/), [Alaska's News Source](https://www.alaskasnewssource.com/2026/09/22/wilson-spars-with-kreiss-tomkins-after-urging-fellow-republicans-suspend-campaigns/)
- 2026-08-18 primary: Kreiss-Tomkins 22.5%, Begich (D) 20.8%, Wilson 10.0%, Bronson 8.1%, Taylor 7.3%. Begich then withdrew and endorsed Kreiss-Tomkins, and Taylor moved up to take his general-election spot. Republican candidates together took well over 40% of primary votes. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_Alaska_gubernatorial_election), [KTOO](https://www.ktoo.org/2026/08/18/kreiss-tomkins-begich-wilson-and-bronson-lead-in-early-governor-primary-results/)

## 4. Base rates
- Alaska has held these statewide RCV general or special elections: the 2022 House special, 2022 House general, 2022 Senate, 2022 governor and 2024 House. In all of them the round-1 leader went on to win:
  - Murkowski led Tshibaka only narrowly in round 1 in 2022 (about 43.4% vs 42.6%) and still won.
  - Dunleavy won in round 1.
  - Peltola led round 1 and won both 2022 House races.
  - Begich led round 1 and won in 2024.
- So the statewide come-from-behind rate in Alaska is 0 of about 5. [2022 Alaska elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Alaska_elections)
- Come-from-behind wins do happen nationally in RCV races (a few percent of multi-round races, per FairVote), and a few Alaska legislative races in 2022 and 2024 saw them. They usually need a round-1 gap of only a few points. The current polling gap here is roughly 16-22 points.
- Transfers between Republicans are not complete: polls project Wilson reaching only 45-48% in the final round.

## 5. Other forecasts
- 2026-10-25 (Kalshi, Alaska Governor winner): Kreiss-Tomkins 0.86, Wilson 0.12, everyone else at or below 0.01. By party: Democratic 0.86, Republican 0.14. Because a Republican win would very likely be a come-from-behind win, these prices roughly track this question.
- Polymarket (Alaska Governor winner): an earlier report put Kreiss-Tomkins at about 79% and Wilson at about 22%. The prices fetched by code only showed long-shot candidates, all at or below 0.001. [FairVote/aggregated search](https://fairvote.org/what-to-expect-in-alaskas-2026-ranked-choice-voting-elections/)
- Polymarket "Closest Governor's Race": Alaska at 0.0235.
- Manifold: Measure 2 (the RCV repeal) at 35%. There is also a Manifold market on how many candidates reach 10% in round 1; I could not get its prices.
- The RealClearPolling average of final-round matchups is Kreiss-Tomkins 53.7, Wilson 46.3. [RCP](https://www.realclearpolling.com/polls/governor/open-primary/2026/alaska)
- I found no market that resolves directly on a "come-from-behind" outcome.

## 6. Upcoming events before resolution
- 2026-11-03: Election Day. Initial first-choice counts come out on election night.
- Absentee ballots postmarked by Election Day can be counted if they arrive within 15 days, until about 2026-11-18. The RCV tabulation usually runs about 15 days after the election, so around 2026-11-18. That is **after** the ~2026-11-10 resolution date, so the final winner may not be official when the question is scheduled to resolve.
- Things that could still move the outcome:
  - late polls;
  - Bronson or Taylor dropping out (they would stay on the ballot, but their votes would consolidate);
  - how many Republican voters rank all three GOP candidates and how many leave ballots unranked ("exhaust");
  - turnout, which Kalshi puts at about 50% to exceed 290K.

**Bottom line:** "Yes" essentially requires a Republican, most likely Wilson, to win on transfers after trailing Kreiss-Tomkins in round 1. Markets put a Republican win at about 12-14%, and polls show Kreiss-Tomkins winning the final round by about 4-10 points.

forecasts.reasoning:
(a) **Timing and what Yes requires.** Election Day is 2026-11-03. First-choice counts come out that night. The RCV tabulation and the official winner likely arrive around 2026-11-18, which is after the nominal resolution date of about 2026-11-10. For Yes, the eventual winner must have trailed another candidate in first-choice votes. In practice that means Wilson (or another Republican) trails Kreiss-Tomkins in round 1, then wins after Bronson's and Taylor's ballots transfer.

(b) **Status quo.** Kreiss-Tomkins leads round 1 by about 20 points and wins the final round by 4 to 10 points. He would be the round-1 leader and the winner, so the question resolves No.

(c) **Base rate.** In Alaska statewide RCV general and special elections, the round-1 leader has won 5 out of 5 times, so the come-from-behind rate is 0 of 5. Nationally, comebacks happen in a few percent of multi-round RCV races, almost always from small round-1 gaps. A gap of 15 points or more almost never gets overturned, but this race is unusual because three Republicans split one bloc. A reasonable structural base rate is about 5 to 10%.

(d) **Evidence.**
- For Yes:
  - Republican candidates combined for over 40% in the August 18 primary.
  - Polls show Republicans splitting about 50% of round-1 votes. Final-round margins are only 4 to 10 points (NYT/Siena, Sep 24 to Oct 1: 52-48; DFP, Oct 8 to 16: 53-47, with a 50-50 scenario).
  - Bronson and Taylor released a late-September video urging voters to rank all three Republicans.
  - Alaska polling has sometimes understated Republicans.
- For No:
  - Kreiss-Tomkins is at 48 to 50% in round 1 (ASR, Oct 15 to 18: 50/30/12/8). Wilson would need near-complete transfers plus a polling miss.
  - He has a large fundraising edge (Oct 6).
  - Kalshi gives Republicans 14% to win (Oct 25).

(e) **Scenarios.**
- No: Kreiss-Tomkins gets about 48% first-choice. Some Bronson and Taylor ballots exhaust, and he wins the final round 53-47.
- Yes: A Republican-leaning polling error puts Kreiss-Tomkins at about 44% and Wilson at 33%. Republicans rank each other heavily, and Wilson wins 51-49 after transfers.

(f) **Reasoning to the final number.** I start from the market's roughly 14% probability of a Republican win. I subtract a small amount for scenarios where a Republican wins while leading round 1, which would resolve No. That is unlikely given a 20-point round-1 gap, so conditional on a Republican win, I put the chance they trailed in round 1 at about 85 to 90%. That gives about 12%. A Kreiss-Tomkins comeback from behind in round 1 adds almost nothing. I stay close to the market anchor.

Probability: 12%

For Yes, the eventual winner must have trailed another candidate in first-choice votes. In practice that means a Republican, most likely Wilson, trails Kreiss-Tomkins in round 1 and then wins on transfers from Bronson and Taylor.

(b) Status quo: Kreiss-Tomkins leads round 1 by about 16-22 points and wins the final round by about 4-10 points. That resolves No.

(c) Base rate:
- In Alaska's statewide RCV races, the round-1 leader won 5 of about 5 times, so the come-from-behind rate is 0 of 5.
- Nationally, come-from-behind wins happen in a few percent of multi-round RCV races, usually when the round-1 gap is small.
- Here the structure is unusual, with one Democrat against three Republicans splitting the vote. That makes a come-from-behind win far more plausible than the generic rate suggests. A better reference point is P(Republican wins), which markets put at about 14%.

(d) Evidence:
- For Yes:
  - Republicans combined lead in round 1 in every poll, about 50-51% across the three Republicans.
  - Bronson and Taylor released a joint video in late September asking Republicans to rank all three GOP candidates.
  - The Data for Progress poll (Oct 8-16) included a 50-50 hypothetical scenario.
  - Alaska leans Republican, and the NYT/Siena poll (Sep 24-Oct 1) had the final round at 52-48.
- For No:
  - The latest ASR poll (Oct 15-18) has Kreiss-Tomkins at 50% in round 1 and 55-45 in the final round.
  - Every final-round poll has Kreiss-Tomkins ahead by 4-10 points.
  - Kalshi (Oct 25) prices the Democrat at 86%.
  - Kreiss-Tomkins out-raised the three Republicans combined (Oct 6).
  - Republican-to-Republican transfers are incomplete because some ballots exhaust.

(e) Scenarios:
- No: Kreiss-Tomkins takes about 48% in round 1, and Republican ballots partially exhaust. He wins the final round 54-46.
- Yes: The polls overstate the Democrat by a few points, as can happen in Alaska. Kreiss-Tomkins gets 46% in round 1 and Wilson 30%. Strong ranking discipline among Republicans carries Wilson to a 50.5-49.5 win after transfers.

(f) I anchor on the market's Republican-win price of 12-14%. I then subtract the small chance that a Republican wins while also leading round 1, which is close to zero given the 20-point gap. I also subtract a negligible amount for edge cases. I do not move much from the market, because it already reflects the polls, and the late ASR poll is slightly unfavorable to Republicans. That gives about 12%.

Probability: 12%

For Yes, the eventual winner must trail another candidate in first-choice votes. In practice, a Republican (most likely Wilson) would have to finish behind Kreiss-Tomkins in round 1 and then overtake him on Bronson and Taylor transfers.

(b) Status quo: Kreiss-Tomkins leads round 1 by roughly 16-22 points, polling at 46-50% first-choice, and wins. That resolves No. A Republican leading round 1 is essentially impossible given the vote split, so a Republican win almost always means Yes.

(c) Base rate: statewide Alaska RCV races have had 0 of 5 come-from-behind winners. Nationally, a few percent of multi-round RCV races see one, usually with round-1 gaps of only a few points. Applied to this situation, the reference class gives roughly 5%. The better anchor is P(Republican wins), which Kalshi prices at 12-14%.

(d) Evidence:
- **For Yes:** Republicans combined poll near 50% of first choices. A Data for Progress hypothetical (Oct 8-16) showed 50-50. Bronson and Taylor urged voters to rank all three Republicans (late September). Alaska polling error could favor Republicans.
- **For No:** ASR (Oct 15-18) puts Kreiss-Tomkins at 50% first-choice and 55-45 in the final round. NYT/Siena (Sep 24-Oct 1) has 52-48 and RCP averages 53.7-46.3. Kreiss-Tomkins has a fundraising edge (Oct 6). Republican transfers are incomplete because of exhausted ballots.

(e) Scenarios:
- **No:** Kreiss-Tomkins gets about 49% in round 1. Many Bronson and Taylor ballots exhaust, and he wins the final round 54-46.
- **Yes:** A polling miss of several points toward Republicans holds Kreiss-Tomkins to about 45% first-choice. Wilson is at 31% and Bronson plus Taylor at 24%, transferring at 80% or better. Wilson wins 51-49 after trailing in round 1.

(f) I start from the market anchor of about 13% for a Republican win, which maps almost one-to-one onto Yes. I shade down slightly for two small leaks: a Republican winner could conceivably lead round 1 if there were a huge polling miss, and Kreiss-Tomkins's first-choice share near 50% gives him a cushion. I do not go below about 10%, because statewide polling error in Alaska is meaningful and log scoring punishes overconfidence.

Probability: 12%

(c) Base rate: Alaska's statewide RCV races have produced 0 of 5 come-from-behind winners. Nationally, about 2-4% of multi-round RCV races are come-from-behind wins, almost always with small round-1 gaps. On that basis the base rate is about 3-5%. However, this race has an unusual structure: one Democrat against three Republicans who are explicitly asking voters to rank each other. That raises the chance of a come-from-behind win well above generic RCV rates.

(d) Evidence:
- **For Yes:**
  - Republicans together poll about 50% in round 1: ASR Oct 15-18 had 30+12+8.
  - The Data for Progress Oct 8-16 hypothetical scenario showed 50-50.
  - NYT/Siena (Sep 24-Oct 1) had the final round at only 52-48.
  - Bronson and Taylor's late-September joint "rank all Republicans" video should improve transfers.

  - Kreiss-Tomkins polls 49-50% in round 1 in the latest polls (ASR, DFP, mid-October). That is near an outright majority.
  - Every poll shows him winning the final round.
  - He has a large fundraising edge: $2.1M versus $852K as of 10-06.
  - Ballot exhaustion among Republican voters limits transfers.

(e) Scenarios:
- **No:** Kreiss-Tomkins gets about 48% in round 1. Republican exhaustion runs at 10-15%, and he wins the final round 54-46.
- **Yes:** A polling miss toward Republicans, similar to past Alaska undercounts of rural or conservative voters, puts Kreiss-Tomkins at about 45% in round 1. Wilson at 31% picks up most Bronson and Taylor transfers and wins 50.5-49.5.

(f) Reasoning to the final number: I start from the Kalshi Republican-win price of 14%, which is a liquid and directly relevant anchor. I subtract the tiny chance that a Republican leads round 1 and wins, which is negligible given a 20-point gap. I also subtract a small amount because the "Republican party" price likely includes some noise. The question's timing does not affect the outcome itself. The result is about 12%.

Probability: 12%

(a) Election Day is 2026-11-03. First-choice counts come out that night, but the official RCV tabulation is likely around 2026-11-18, which is after the nominal resolution date of about 2026-11-10. For Yes, the eventual winner must have trailed another candidate in initial first-choice votes. In practice that means a Republican, most likely Wilson, finishes behind Kreiss-Tomkins in round 1 and then overtakes him on transfers from Bronson and Taylor.

(b) Status quo: Kreiss-Tomkins leads round 1 by about 16-22 points and also leads the final round by about 4-10 points in polling. He would win as the round-1 leader, which resolves No.

(c) Base rate: In Alaska's statewide RCV races (2022 House special, 2022 House general, 2022 Senate, 2022 governor, 2024 House), the round-1 leader won 0 of 5 times as a come-from-behind... more precisely, a trailing candidate won 0 of 5 times. Nationally, come-from-behind wins happen in a few percent of multi-round RCV races, almost always with small round-1 gaps. The generic base rate is about 3-5%. This race is structurally unusual, though: three Republicans split one bloc against a single Democrat. That makes the useful reference the probability of a Republican win, which markets put at 12-14%.

(d) Evidence for Yes:
- Republicans together took well over 40% of the 2026-08-18 primary vote.
- On 2026-09-26, Bronson and Taylor ran a joint video urging voters to rank all three Republicans.
- Data for Progress (Oct 8-16) showed one scenario at 50-50.
- Alaska polls have sometimes underestimated Republicans.
- NYT/Siena (Sep 24-Oct 1) had the final round at only 52-48.

Evidence for No:
- ASR (Oct 15-18) had Kreiss-Tomkins at 50 in round 1 and winning the final round 55-45.
- The RCP final-round average is 53.7-46.3.
- Ballot exhaustion limits how many Republican votes transfer.
- Kreiss-Tomkins had a large fundraising edge as of 2026-10-06.
- Kalshi prices the Democratic party at 0.86.

(e) No scenario: Kreiss-Tomkins gets about 49% in round 1, some Bronson and Taylor ballots exhaust, and he wins the final round by about 6 points. Yes scenario: a polling miss of 4-6 points toward Republicans leaves Kreiss-Tomkins at about 46% in round 1. Republican voters rank all three, and Wilson overtakes him after transfers, winning about 51-49.

(f) I start from the market-implied Republican win probability of 12-14%. A Republican win almost always means a come-from-behind win, since no Republican is near leading round 1. I subtract a tiny amount for the remote case where a Republican leads round 1 and wins, which would resolve No. I add a little for a possible Republican-leaning polling error in Alaska. The net is roughly the market figure.

Probability: 12%
